newsitem.title: UK: Indium firms in minor metals, producers up price.
newsitem.headline: Indium firms in minor metals, producers up price.

text.p: Indium held the spotlight of the industrial minor metals over the past week as brisk Japanese demand against the backdrop of a lack of readily available material drove prices higher.
Meanwhile, producers raised their list prices, with Indium Corp upping its level by $30 to $290/a kilo, while Arconium went to $8.10 a troy ounce.
Elsewhere, traders failed to find middle ground in the antimony market, while cobalt firmed on consumer business and found background support from the turmoil in Zaire.
Free-market indium continued to trade above $300 a kilo and looked poised to move towards $400 a kilo near-term as major producer China failed to sell into the market.
Traders suggested that China was sold out or had started to hold back any available stock in anticipation of higher prices.
Western and Peruvian producers were also said to be running low stocks or were sold out completely.
"At present demand is far out-stripping supply," one trader said.

Traders said China now held the key to the indium market. Several suggested that they believed material held by China was of small amounts. "Even if they release it I fear it will not be enough to meet demand.
Traders noted that the US stockpile recently sold just over one tonne of indium. The sale exhausted the amount of indium authorised for sale in the current fiscal year.

Longs and shorts locked horns in the antimony market. Business ranged between $2,150 to $2,060 a tonne. Bulls of the market said that the lower end did not reflect the true market as the material was of very poor quality.
They said shorts and maybe some consumers were talking the market down before covering.
Others argued that the higher numbers mentioned were largely due to market manouevering by operators holding long positions.
On Friday the US Stockpile sold 60 tonnes of antimony at around $2,000 a tonne.
European cobalt prices remained steady and were looking to probe higher against the backdrop of consumer enquiry. Background support was found from the continued unrest in Zaire, traders said.
Rebel forces since October 1996 have been in conflict with government troops and are now threatening to move deeper into the mineral-rich Shaba province.
At present Zaire produces around 5,000 tonnes of cobalt and 40,000 tonnes of copper.
Cobalt prices after recent downside pressure are starting to climb on supply/demand pressures, traders said.
Several suggested that demand would outstrip production against the backdrop of offtake from the aerospace industry and battery production.
At the moment it is in the hands of how consumers will react to market fundamentals and their medium-term commitments.
Recently enquiry from end-users was at a low ebb but it is starting to turn, traders said.
The latest DLA tender result for 1.1 million lbs of lower grade cobalt has been delayed but is due on March 27. On March 31 bids will be due for 1 million pounds of higher grade DLA cobalt.
